title: Two Entrances and Four Practices (Erru sixing lun)
alt_titles: Putidamo lüe bian dasheng rudao sixing 菩提達磨略辨大乘入道四行
Erzhong ru 二種入 (in the Shaoshi liumen)

attribution.tradition: Bodhidharma's teaching, recorded with a preface by his disciple Tanlin
attribution.scholarly: widely accepted as the earliest stratum of Chan teaching, 6th c.; the longer Dunhuang 'Long Scroll' adds later dialogues

scholarly.text: 6th c. core; summary already in Daoxuan's Xu gaoseng zhuan (645)

structure.description: short treatise: preface, the two entrances, the four practices; Dunhuang versions append letters and dialogues

summary: Distinguishes entry by principle (liru) — through the teaching awakening to the one true nature shared by all beings, obscured by adventitious dust, and 'abiding firmly in wall-gazing' — from entry by practice (xingru), comprising four practices: requiting enmity, according with conditions, seeking nothing, and according with the Dharma.

title: Inscription on Faith in Mind (Xinxin ming)

attribution.scholarly: attribution doubted; probably 8th c., close in wording to the Oxhead Xinming

structure.description: about 146 four-character lines (the Taishō text shows 145 lines, 580 characters)

summary: A poem in four-character lines on non-duality: 'The supreme Way is not difficult; it only dislikes picking and choosing.' Grasping, rejecting and dualistic views are the mind's sickness; when one mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault; faith in mind is non-dual.

title: Treatise on the Essentials of Cultivating the Mind (Xiuxin yao lun)
alt_titles: Zuishangsheng lun 最上乘論 (Taishō title)

attribution.scholarly: compiled by Hongren's disciples, early 8th c.

summary: In question-and-answer form, teaches that guarding the original true mind (shou benzhen xin) is the root of nirvāṇa and the essential gate of the Way: when deluded thoughts do not arise and the sense of 'mine' ceases, one is equal to the buddhas.

title: Treatise on Contemplating the Mind (Guanxin lun)
alt_titles: Poxiang lun 破相論 (the same text under Bodhidharma's name, in the Shaoshi liumen)

attribution.tradition: transmitted in later Chan under Bodhidharma's name as the Poxiang lun
attribution.scholarly: by Shenxiu, as identified from Dunhuang manuscripts and early catalogues

summary: Teaches that contemplating the mind alone comprehends all practices; reinterprets merit-making, the precepts and rituals as inner mental acts.
notes: Dunhuang text (T85 no. 2833) not held locally; the Poxiang lun version is in Shaoshi liumen T2009 (local, not yet read for this entry).

title: Expedient Means of Attaining the Unborn in the Mahāyāna (Dasheng wusheng fangbian men)
summary: Northern-school manual presenting five expedient means (wu fangbian), beginning with 'viewing purity' and 'separating from thoughts' (linian), correlated with the Awakening of Faith, the Lotus, the Vimalakīrti, the Viśeṣacintā and the Avataṃsaka.
notes: Dunhuang (T85 no. 2834); not held locally. Details of the five means from memory — low confidence.

title: Record of the Masters and Disciples of the Laṅkāvatāra (Lengqie shizi ji)
summary: Early Chan lineage history presenting Guṇabhadra, translator of the Laṅkāvatāra, as first master and Bodhidharma as second, through Huike, Sengcan, Daoxin, Hongren and Shenxiu; includes Daoxin's teaching on guarding the one and one-practice samādhi.
notes: Dunhuang (T85 no. 2837); not held locally.

title: Annals of the Transmission of the Dharma Treasure (Chuan fabao ji)
summary: Early lineage history by the layman Du Fei, beginning the Chinese line with Bodhidharma and ending with Faru and Shenxiu.
notes: Dunhuang (T85 no. 2838); not held locally.

title: Record of the Dharma Jewel through the Generations (Lidai fabao ji)
summary: Baotang history tracing the robe of Bodhidharma from Huineng through Empress Wu to Zhishen, Chuji, Musang and Wuzhu; records Musang's three phrases (no remembering, no thinking, no forgetting) and Wuzhu's rejection of ritual practice.

title: Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch (Liuzu tanjing)

attribution.tradition: sermons of Huineng recorded by his disciple Fahai
attribution.scholarly: the earliest (Dunhuang) version dates from c. 780 and shows Heze (Shenhui) interests; the text grew through the Huixin (967), Qisong (1056), Deyi (1290) and Zongbao (1291) editions

structure.description: Zongbao edition: prefaces and ten chapters (行由, 般若, 疑問, 定慧, 坐禪, 懺悔, 機緣, 頓漸, 宣詔, 付囑) plus appendices

summary: The Sixth Patriarch Huineng's autobiography and sermons at the Dafan temple: the verse contest with Shenxiu, the secret transmission of robe and Dharma, the sudden teaching that the self-nature is originally pure, samādhi and prajñā as one like lamp and light, no-thought as tenet, no-form as substance and non-abiding as root, seated meditation redefined, the formless repentance, vows and refuges, the encounters with disciples, and the thirty-six pairs of opposites.

title: Dunhuang Platform Sūtra
title_original: 南宗頓教最上大乘摩訶般若波羅蜜經六祖惠能大師於韶州大梵寺施法壇經

attribution.scholarly: compiled in Heze (Shenhui) circles or a related Southern-school milieu, c. 780

structure.description: 57 sections in the CBETA division (第一折–第五十七折)

summary: The earliest extant recension: Huineng's account of his life and the verse contest (with two verses by Huineng), the formless precepts, samādhi and prajñā as one, no-thought, seated meditation, the three bodies, four vows, repentance and refuges, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā sermon, answers to Prefect Wei, disciples' encounters, a prophecy of a champion twenty years after Huineng's death, the patriarchs' transmission verses, and the insistence that possession of the Platform Sūtra itself marks true transmission.

title: Treatise Establishing the True and False in the Southern School of Bodhidharma (Putidamo nanzong ding shifei lun)
title_original: 菩提達摩南宗定是非論
summary: Record of Shenhui's public challenge at the Great Assembly of Huatai (732) to the Northern school: Shenxiu's line is collateral, Bodhidharma's robe passed to Huineng, and the Northern teaching of 'freezing the mind to enter samādhi, fixing the mind to view purity, stirring the mind to illumine outward, collecting the mind to realise inwardly' is gradual.
notes: Dunhuang manuscripts (ed. Hu Shi); not held locally. The four-phrase characterisation of Northern practice (凝心入定，住心看淨，起心外照，攝心內證) is quoted from memory — moderate confidence.

title: Miscellaneous Dialogues of the Reverend of Nanyang (Shenhui)
summary: Shenhui's dialogues with officials and monks on sudden awakening, no-thought, the identity of samādhi and prajñā, and the empty and calm knowing of the mind.
notes: Dunhuang; not held locally.

title: Platform Talk of Shenhui (Tanyu)
title_original: 南陽和上頓教解脫禪門直了性壇語
summary: Shenhui's sermon at an ordination platform: the three trainings of precepts, samādhi and prajñā defined in terms of no-thought; seeing the nature; sudden awakening.
notes: Dunhuang; not held locally; low confidence on details.

title: Record Manifesting the Teaching (Xianzong ji)
alt_titles: Heze dashi xianzong ji 荷澤大師顯宗記

attribution.scholarly: a Dunhuang fragment (Dunwu wusheng boruo song) corresponds; attribution generally accepted with reservation

summary: A short statement of Heze teaching: no-thought is the tenet and non-action the root, true emptiness is the substance and wondrous being the function; samādhi and wisdom are identical; the six perfections are complete in the non-dual gate.

title: Song of Realizing the Way (Zhengdao ge)

attribution.tradition: by Yongjia Xuanjue, awakened in one night at Caoxi
attribution.scholarly: authorship questioned; the song may date from the later 8th c.

summary: A long song of awakening: the leisurely person of the Way beyond learning neither removes deluded thoughts nor seeks the true; the real nature of ignorance is buddha-nature; walking is Chan, sitting is Chan; the one nature pervades all natures, one moon appears in all waters.

summary: Yongjia Xuanjue's meditation treatise in ten sections, rooted in Tiantai calming and contemplation: e.g. alertness (xingxing) and calm (jijing) must be balanced — calm without alertness is dullness, alertness without calm is scattered thought.

title: Harmony of Difference and Sameness (Cantongqi / Sandōkai)

structure.description: 44 lines of five characters (220 characters) as in Jingde chuandeng lu juan 30

summary: Shitou Xiqian's poem of 44 five-character lines: the mind of the great sage of India was intimately transmitted east and west; the numinous source is bright and pure while its branches flow in the dark; each gate and object interfuses and does not interfuse; light and dark are like the front and back foot in walking.

title: Song of the Precious Mirror Samādhi (Baojing sanmei ge)

attribution.tradition: transmitted from Yunyan to Dongshan, who passed it to Caoshan
attribution.scholarly: first attested in Song sources; authorship uncertain

summary: Dongshan's song on the Dharma secretly entrusted by buddhas and patriarchs: like snow in a silver bowl, like a heron hidden in moonlight; 'you are not it, it is just you'; the hexagram of double fire folds into three and turns into five (the five ranks); the practice is hidden and intimate, 'like a fool, like an idiot'.

scholarly.text: compilations of the 17th–18th c. drawing on Song sources

summary: The sayings and encounters of Dongshan Liangjie: his questions on the preaching of the insentient, his awakening on seeing his reflection while crossing a stream, the five ranks of lord and minister, the five ranks of merit, the three leaks, and the Precious Mirror Samādhi.

summary: Caoshan Benji's sayings, including his explanation of the five ranks as lord and minister: the real position is the realm of emptiness, the apparent position the realm of form; their union is the 'combined' rank.

title: Extensive Record of Mazu Daoyi (Mazu yulu)

attribution.scholarly: a Song compilation (in the Sijia yulu); earlier material in the Zutang ji and Jingde chuandeng lu

summary: Mazu's sermons and encounters: 'this very mind is buddha', 'neither mind nor buddha', 'the ordinary mind is the Way', 'the Way needs no cultivation — only do not defile it'.
notes: Not in the local Taishō volumes (Xuzangjing X69); Mazu's sermon is read locally in Jingde chuandeng lu juan 28.

title: Extensive Record of Baizhang (Baizhang guanglu)
summary: Baizhang Huaihai's sermons on not being attached to existence or non-existence, the three phrases (initial, middle, final good), and the fox kōan.
notes: Not held locally (Xuzangjing).

title: Regulations of the Chan School (Chanmen guishi)

attribution.scholarly: a Song-period description (1004) of what was believed to be Baizhang's system; no Tang text of a Baizhang code survives

summary: A short account of Baizhang's founding of separate Chan monasteries: an abbot called 'elder' living in the 'ten-foot square', no Buddha hall but a Dharma hall, a common Sangha hall where monks sit and sleep by seniority, morning and evening assemblies, the 'universal invitation' to communal labour (puqing) with high and low sharing the work, and ten offices.

title: Imperial Edition of Baizhang's Pure Rules (Chixiu Baizhang qinggui)
summary: Yuan-dynasty comprehensive monastic code compiled under imperial order: rites for the emperor and patriarchs, the abbot, officers, daily and annual observances, communal labour (puqing), funerals of monks; it repeats the saying 'a day without work, a day without food'.

title: Pure Rules of the Chan Monastery (Chanyuan qinggui)
summary: The oldest extant Chan monastic code (1103), by Changlu Zongze: offices, daily routine, rites, meals, meditation, and the 'Principles of Seated Meditation' (Zuochan yi).
notes: Not held locally (Xuzangjing X63).

title: Principles of Seated Meditation (Zuochan yi)
summary: The earliest Chan manual of seated meditation: arouse compassion and vow, regulate food and sleep, sit in the full or half lotus with the body upright, let go of all involvements; 'when a thought arises, be aware of it; when you are aware of it, it vanishes'; meditation is the Dharma gate of ease and joy.
notes: Dōgen's Fukanzazengi draws on it. Wording of the quoted line is from memory — no original given.

title: Essentials of the Transmission of Mind (Chuanxin fayao)
title_original: 黃檗山斷際禪師傳心法要

scholarly.text: teaching c. 842–848; preface by Pei Xiu dated 857

summary: Huangbo Xiyun's teaching as recorded by the minister Pei Xiu: all buddhas and sentient beings are only the one mind; this mind is buddha; seeking outward with form is error; no-mind (wuxin) is the Way; the dying should see the five aggregates as empty and neither follow good visions nor fear bad ones.

summary: Further dialogues of Huangbo recorded by Pei Xiu at Wanling, ending with the verse: 'unless the cold once pierces to the bone, how could the plum blossom's fragrance strike the nose?'

title: Treatise on the Essential Gate of Entering the Way through Sudden Awakening (Dunwu rudao yaomen lun)
summary: Dazhu Huihai's catechism: sudden awakening means suddenly ending deluded thoughts and awakening to non-attainment; seated meditation is no-thought; samādhi and prajñā are equal.
notes: Not held locally (Xuzangjing).

attribution.scholarly: the standard text is the 1120 edition of Yuanjue Zongyan; earlier material in the Zutang ji (952), Jingde chuandeng lu (1004) and Tiansheng guangdeng lu (1036)

structure.description: prefaces; sermons (上堂, 示眾); critical examinations (勘辨); record of pilgrimage (行錄); stele

summary: Sermons, encounters and biography of Linji Yixuan: the true person of no rank; 'just you, listening to the Dharma'; the four classifications of person and environment; the three phrases, three mysteries and three essentials; the four shouts; be master wherever you are; 'if you meet the Buddha, kill the Buddha'; his awakening at Dayu's words about Huangbo.

title: Ten Guidelines for the Chan School (Zongmen shigui lun)
summary: Fayan Wenyi's critique of the faults of Chan teachers of his time: not having clarified the mind-ground yet teaching, partisanship among houses, not knowing the devices of the five houses, ignoring the scriptures, reciting old cases without insight, composing verses without principle, and similar abuses.
notes: Not held locally; the list of ten is summarised from memory — details low confidence.

title: Eyes of Humans and Gods (Rentian yanmu)
summary: Compendium of the teaching devices of the Five Houses: Linji's four classifications, three mysteries and three essentials, four guest-host relations; Caodong's five ranks; Yunmen's three phrases; Guiyang's circle-figures; Fayan's six characteristics.

structure.description: 30 fascicles; traditionally 1,701 persons (the source of the phrase 'the 1,700 kōans')

summary: The canonical Chan genealogy (1004) by Daoyuan: the seven buddhas, 28 Indian and six Chinese patriarchs, and the collateral and main lines of Tang and Five Dynasties masters with their encounter dialogues, followed by sermons, verses and inscriptions (juan 27–30).

title: Compendium of the Five Lamps (Wudeng huiyuan)

title: Baolin Biographies (Baolin zhuan)

structure.description: 10 pictures, each with a prose preface and a verse

summary: Kuoan Shiyuan's ten pictures with verses (and prose prefaces by his disciple Ciyuan): 1 searching for the ox, 2 seeing the traces, 3 seeing the ox, 4 catching the ox, 5 herding the ox, 6 riding the ox home, 7 ox forgotten, self remains, 8 ox and self both forgotten, 9 returning to the origin, 10 entering the marketplace with helping hands.
notes: Not held locally (Xuzangjing X64). The path map pth:ten-oxherding-pictures is owned by U51; this unit supplies the source and teachings.

title: Essentials of Chan (Chanyao) of Gaofeng
summary: Gaofeng Yuanmiao's instructions on huatou practice: great faith, great doubt and great determination (or 'great anger') as the three essentials; one of the four texts of the Korean curriculum (Seonyo).

title: General Preface to the Collection of Expressions of the Chan Source (Chanyuan zhuquanji duxu)
summary: Zongmi's preface (c. 833) to his lost anthology of Chan writings: correlates three Chan tenets (stopping the false and cultivating mind; eliminating traces; directly revealing the mind-nature) with three teachings, defends sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation, and identifies the mind's essence as 'empty and calm knowing' — 'the one word knowing is the gate of all wonders'.

title: Determination of the True Principle of Sudden Awakening in the Mahāyāna (Dunwu dasheng zhengli jue)
summary: Wangxi's Chinese record of the Chan master Moheyan's answers to Indian critics at the Tibetan court (late 8th c.): not thinking, not examining (bu si bu guan) as the way to reveal the originally pure mind.

summary: A Chan lexicon (1108) by Muan Shanqing, the earliest source generally cited for the complete four-line formula 'a separate transmission outside the teachings, not dependent on words and letters, pointing directly at the human mind, seeing the nature and becoming a buddha'.
notes: Not held locally; the claim about the first full formula is the common scholarly account — moderate confidence.

alt_titles: Goryeoguk Bojo seonsa susim kyol 高麗國普照禪師修心訣
summary: Jinul's primer: the buddha is one's own mind; the empty and calm, numinous awareness that asks the question is one's original face; the path is sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation, like an infant who has all its faculties but must grow; cultivation after awakening is the balanced keeping of samādhi and prajñā; supernatural powers are secondary and appear only through gradual cultivation.

title: Excerpts from the Dharma Collection and Special Practice Record, with Personal Notes (Jeoryo)
title_original: 法集別行錄節要并入私記
summary: Jinul's last major work (1209): a commentary on Zongmi's comparison of the four Chan schools, affirming Heze's sudden awakening/gradual cultivation as a basis while ending with Dahui's shortcut of the hwadu for those who can use it; one of the four texts of the Korean curriculum.
notes: Not held locally.

title: Resolving Doubts about Observing the Hwadu (Ganhwa gyeoruiron)
summary: Jinul's posthumously published (1215) treatise defending the hwadu shortcut against doctrinal objections: it bypasses the 'dead words' of doctrinal understanding and uses the 'live word'; it lists the defects to avoid in contemplating 'wu'.
notes: Not held locally.

title: Complete and Sudden Attainment of Buddhahood (Wondon seongbullon)
summary: Jinul's treatise (posthumous 1215) harmonising Seon with Li Tongxuan's Huayan: ordinary beings' own 'unmoving wisdom' is the buddha of immovable wisdom; faith in this is the entry to the complete-sudden teaching.
notes: Not held locally.

title: Encouragement to Practice: the Compact of the Samādhi and Prajñā Community
summary: Jinul's manifesto (1190) calling monks to form a retreat community devoted to the balanced cultivation of samādhi and prajñā, and answering Pure Land and doctrinal objections.
notes: Not held locally.

title: Collection of Seon Cases with Verse Comments (Seonmun yeomsong jip)
summary: Hyesim's great kōan anthology (1226): 1,125 cases with verses and comments by Chinese and Korean masters.
notes: Not held locally; number of cases from memory.

title: Mirror for Seon Students (Seon'ga gwigam)
summary: Hyujeong's handbook (1564): Seon is the Buddha's mind and the teachings his words; one should first understand through the teachings and then enter Seon through the live word of the hwadu; practice requires great faith, great doubt and great determination; also on precepts, recitation and conduct.
notes: Not held locally.

title: The Correct Path of the Seon School (Seonmun jeongno)
summary: Seongcheol's polemic (1981) arguing that true awakening is sudden awakening with sudden cultivation (dono donsu) and that Jinul's sudden awakening/gradual cultivation describes only 'understanding-awakening' (haeo).

title: Treatise on Promoting Zen for the Protection of the Country (Kōzen gokoku ron)
summary: Eisai's defence (1198) of Zen against the Tendai establishment: Zen is the source of all Buddhist teachings and was part of Saichō's own heritage; strict observance of the precepts is its foundation (against the Daruma school); promoting Zen protects the state.
notes: Not held locally (T80 no. 2543).

title: Drinking Tea for Nourishing Life (Kissa yōjōki)
summary: Eisai's treatise (1211, revised 1214) on tea as medicine that strengthens the heart, with mulberry as a remedy.
notes: Not held locally.

title: Treasury of the True Dharma Eye (Shōbōgenzō)

structure.description: compiled as a 75-fascicle version and a 12-fascicle version (Dōgen's late revision), later combined in the 95-fascicle Honzan edition (1815)

summary: Dōgen's Japanese-language essays (1231–1253) on the buddha-way: zazen as the realization of buddhahood, the realized kōan, being-time, buddha-nature, dharma transmission, the monastic life, cause and effect, and the teachings of the ancestors.
notes: Not held locally (T82 no. 2582). Fascicles are entered as separate sources with part_of src:shobogenzo.

title: Genjōkōan (The Realized Kōan)
summary: When all dharmas are buddha-dharma there is delusion and awakening; carrying the self forward to verify the myriad things is delusion, the myriad things advancing and verifying the self is awakening; to study the buddha-way is to study the self, to study the self is to forget the self, to forget the self is to be verified by the myriad dharmas; firewood does not become ash; awakening is like the moon reflected in water; the fan of Mayu Baoche — the wind-nature is everywhere, yet one fans.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Bendōwa (Talk on Wholehearted Practice)
summary: The self-fulfilling samādhi (jijuyū zanmai) transmitted by buddhas is right sitting; practice and realization are one (shushō ittō), so even a beginner's wholehearted practice is the whole of original realization; rejects the view that the mind-nature is permanent while the body perishes (the Śreṇika heresy); answers eighteen questions.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Uji (Being-Time)
summary: 'Being-time' means time is already being and all being is time; each moment abides in its own dharma position; time 'flows' (kyōryaku) from today to tomorrow and from today to yesterday.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Busshō (Buddha-Nature)
summary: Reads the Nirvāṇa-sūtra line as 'all sentient beings — whole being — is buddha-nature' (shitsuu busshō); rejects buddha-nature as a seed or as a permanent self; impermanence is buddha-nature; discusses Zhaozhou's and Guishan's 'no buddha-nature'.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Zazenshin (Lancet of Seated Meditation)
summary: Comments on Yaoshan's 'thinking of not-thinking… non-thinking' and on Nanyue polishing a tile; praises Hongzhi's Zuochan zhen and offers Dōgen's own version.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Zazengi (Principles of Zazen, Shōbōgenzō)
summary: Short instructions: a quiet place, thick mat, full or half lotus, cosmic mudrā, upright posture, breathing through the nose, thinking of not-thinking; 'zazen is not learning meditation (shūzen); it is the Dharma gate of ease and joy'.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Sokushin zebutsu (This Very Mind is Buddha)
summary: Rejects reading Mazu's 'this very mind is buddha' as the Śreṇika view of an eternal knowing mind; mind is mountains, rivers and the great earth.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Ikka myōju (One Bright Pearl)
summary: On Xuansha's saying 'the whole ten-direction world is one bright pearl'.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Raihai tokuzui (Paying Homage and Obtaining the Marrow)
summary: One should bow to whoever has attained the Way, whether man or woman, old or young; criticises exclusion of women from sacred places and from teaching.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Shukke kudoku (The Merit of Leaving Home)
summary: Twelve-fascicle essay insisting that leaving household life and receiving the precepts is essential to realizing the buddha-way.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Jinshin inga (Deep Faith in Cause and Effect)
summary: Twelve-fascicle essay rejecting the view that the awakened are free from causality: Baizhang's fox shows 'not obscuring cause and effect', and denial of causality is a grave wrong view.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Daishugyō (Great Practice)
summary: Earlier essay on the fox kōan, reading 'not falling' and 'not obscuring' as both expressions of great practice.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Gyōji (Continuous Practice)
summary: Buddhas and ancestors sustain continuous practice that is not interrupted; stories of ancestors' practice.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Shōji (Birth and Death)
summary: Because there is buddha in birth-and-death there is no birth-and-death; birth-and-death is the life of the buddha; neither cling nor reject; throw body and mind into the house of the buddha.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Sansuikyō (Mountains and Waters Sūtra)
summary: The mountains and waters of the present are the expression of the ancient buddhas' way; 'the blue mountains are always walking'.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Keisei sanshoku (Sounds of the Valley Streams, Colours of the Mountains)
summary: Su Dongpo's awakening verse — the valley streams are the Buddha's long tongue, the mountains his pure body; exhortation to arouse the mind of the Way.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Shinjin gakudō (Study of the Way with Body and Mind)
summary: The Way is studied with the mind and with the body.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Maka hannya haramitsu (Mahāprajñāpāramitā)
summary: Commentary on the Heart Sūtra: the five aggregates are five instances of prajñā.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Hachidainingaku (Eight Awarenesses of Great Beings)
summary: Dōgen's last work, on the eight awarenesses from the Sūtra of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching: few desires, contentment, enjoying tranquillity, diligence, not forgetting mindfulness, samādhi, wisdom, no idle talk.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Shisho (Document of Heritage)
summary: On the dharma-transmission documents Dōgen saw in China and their meaning: buddhas alone transmit to buddhas.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Menju (Face-to-Face Transmission)
summary: Transmission occurs face to face between buddha and buddha; Dōgen's own face-to-face reception from Rujing in 1225.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Kesa kudoku (The Merit of the Robe)
summary: The kāṣāya is the body and mind of the Buddha; on its sewing, wearing and veneration.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Universally Recommended Instructions for Zazen (Fukanzazengi)
summary: Dōgen's first instruction (in Chinese, 1227; autograph Tenpuku manuscript 1233; later revised) on seated meditation: the Way is fundamentally complete, so why practise? — yet the slightest gap and heaven and earth are separated; step back and turn the light inward; sit in full or half lotus, upright; think of not-thinking — how? — non-thinking; this is the essential art of zazen; zazen is not learning meditation but the Dharma gate of ease and joy.
notes: Not held locally; the not-thinking passage quotes Yaoshan (read locally in Jingde chuandeng lu juan 14).

title: Extensive Record of Eihei (Eihei kōroku)
summary: Dōgen's Chinese-language Dharma-hall discourses, informal talks, verses and kōan comments, compiled by his disciples.

title: Record of Things Heard from the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye (Shōbōgenzō zuimonki)
summary: Ejō's notes (1235–1238) of Dōgen's informal talks: give up body and life for the Dharma, practise just sitting, abandon fame and gain.

title: Instructions for the Cook (Tenzo kyōkun)
summary: Dōgen's instructions (1237) for the monastery cook: kitchen work done with joyful, nurturing and great mind is the buddha-way; his meetings with Chinese tenzo.

title: Pure Rules of Eihei (Eihei shingi)
summary: Collection (published 1667) of six of Dōgen's monastic instructions, including Tenzo kyōkun and Fushukuhanpō (meal procedure).

title: Record of the Hōkyō Era (Hōkyōki)
summary: Dōgen's notes of his questions to Rujing (1225–1227), including Rujing's teaching that sitting in meditation is dropping off body and mind, and that burning incense, prostrations, recitation of Buddha's name, repentance and sūtra reading are unnecessary.

title: Points to Watch in Studying the Way (Gakudō yōjinshū)
summary: Dōgen's ten points (1234) for practitioners: arouse bodhi-mind, seek a true teacher, practise with body and mind.

title: Three Hundred Cases of the True Dharma Eye (Shōbōgenzō sanbyakusoku)
summary: Dōgen's collection (1235) of 300 kōans in Chinese (the 'Mana Shōbōgenzō').

title: Record of the Transmission of Light (Denkōroku)
summary: Keizan's lectures (1300) on the awakening of each of the 53 ancestors from Śākyamuni through Mahākāśyapa, the Indian and Chinese patriarchs, Dōgen and Ejō.

title: Points to Watch in Zazen (Zazen yōjinki)
summary: Keizan's practical instructions on zazen: posture, eyes, diet, clothing; ordinarily rest the mind in the left palm — if the mind sinks, place it at the hairline or between the eyebrows, if it scatters, at the tip of the nose or below the navel; warns against visionary and other deviant states.

title: Pure Rules of Keizan (Keizan shingi)
summary: Keizan's monastic code (1324) for Yōkōji, incorporating esoteric and devotional rites.

title: Dialogues in a Dream (Muchū mondō)
summary: Musō Soseki's answers (1344) to Ashikaga Tadayoshi on Zen practice, prayer, merit and expedient means.

title: Crazy Cloud Anthology (Kyōunshū)
summary: Ikkyū Sōjun's Chinese poems, including satire of hypocritical Zen and poems on love and freedom.

title: Mud and Water from Enzan (Enzan wadei gassui shū)
summary: Bassui Tokushō's teachings (1386): ask yourself 'who is the master who sees and hears?'; deep doubt about one's own mind leads to seeing the nature.

title: Record of the Mysterious Workings of Immovable Wisdom (Fudōchi shinmyōroku)
summary: Takuan Sōhō's letter to the swordsman Yagyū Munenori: the mind must not stop anywhere; immovable wisdom moves freely without abiding.

title: Sermons of Bankei (Bankei zenji seppō)
summary: Bankei Yōtaku's vernacular sermons: everyone is born with the unborn buddha-mind, which illuminates everything; do not turn it into anger or desire; no need for kōan struggle — simply abide in the Unborn.

title: Donkey-Saddle Bridge (Roankyō)
summary: Suzuki Shōsan's sayings compiled by Echū (1660): 'guardian-king (niō) Zen', practising with fierce energy; death contemplation.

title: Right Action for All (Banmin tokuyō)
summary: Shōsan's teaching that each occupation — warrior, farmer, artisan, merchant — is buddha-practice.

title: Idle Talk on a Night Boat (Yasenkanna)

attribution.tradition: Hakuin's own account of meeting Hakuyū
attribution.scholarly: Hakuyū (Ishikawa Jishun) is historical, but the meeting as narrated is regarded as partly literary

summary: Hakuin's account (1757) of the 'Zen sickness' he contracted from excessive practice and its cure learned from the hermit Hakuyū: introspection (naikan) concentrating the breath and energy in the lower abdomen (tanden, kikai), and the soft-butter method of visualised healing; warns that the method is for restoring health so that practice can continue.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory.

title: Embossed Tea Kettle (Orategama)
summary: Hakuin's letters (1749–1751) to a feudal lord and others: the importance of practice in the midst of activity over quiet sitting, the naikan method, and nenbutsu and kōan.

title: Song in Praise of Zazen (Zazen wasan)
summary: Hakuin's vernacular hymn: all beings are originally buddhas, like water and ice; not knowing it is near they seek it far away; the Mahāyāna zazen is beyond praise; this very place is the Lotus Land, this very body the Buddha.

title: The Sound of One Hand (Sekishu onjō)
summary: Hakuin's piece (1753) introducing his kōan 'hear the sound of one hand', which he found more effective than 'wu' for raising the great doubt.

title: Wild Ivy (Itsumadegusa)
summary: Hakuin's autobiography (1766): his fear of hell, great doubt, first awakening at the sound of a temple bell, humbling by Shōju Rōjin, Zen sickness and later awakenings.

title: Discourse on the Inexhaustible Lamp of the Zen School (Shūmon mujintō ron)
summary: Tōrei Enji's systematic presentation (written 1751, published 1800) of Zen practice in stages: faith, seeing the nature, advanced practice, transmission and teaching.

title: Pure Rules of Ōbaku (Ōbaku shingi)
summary: Ōbaku monastic code (1672) compiled under Ingen, with Ming-style ordination, chanting and ritual.

title: Kenzeiki
summary: Biography of Dōgen (1452) by the Eiheiji abbot Kenzei; a principal source of the tradition's account of Dōgen's life.

title: Zen Phrase Anthology (Zenrin kushū)
summary: Anthology of Chinese phrases used as capping phrases (jakugo) in Rinzai kōan training; the 1688 edition expands Tōyō Eichō's earlier Kuzōshi.

title: Collection of Entangling Vines (Shūmon kattōshū)
summary: Rinzai kōan collection (1689) of 272 cases used in training.
notes: Number of cases from memory — low confidence.
